prompt: One fault always causes exactly one failure.
confirm: One fault can cause several failures, or none at all.
explanation: Faults and failures are many-to-many: one fault can trigger several different failures, a fault may never trigger any, and several faults can combine into one failure.

prompt: Which testing level checks an individual component in isolation?

distractor.1: System testing checks the whole product, not one unit.
distractor.2: Acceptance checks user needs, much later.
distractor.3: Regression re-runs old tests after changes.

explanation: Unit testing targets individual components or submodules; the larger scales (integration, system, acceptance) build on top of it.

prompt: Put the EP recipe in order.
instructions: Drag the rows into the correct sequence.
explanation: Understand, categorise, cover each category once, then concretise with data and expected results.

prompt: The categories x < 0 and x < 100 are proposed for one input. What is wrong?
options: They overlap: some inputs fit both

distractor.1: There is no OR keyword; the problem is overlap.
distractor.2: Both are numeric ranges, not syntax tests.
distractor.3: Completeness is not the issue; mutual exclusion is.

explanation: x = -5 fits both categories, so failures cannot be attributed. Rewrite as x < 0 versus 0 <= x < 100.

instructions: Drag each word into its blank.
text: Every ___ contributes ___ test values, one from each ___.
explanation: A boundary sits between two categories and the fault could lie on either side, so both sides donate a value.

prompt: Why do faults cluster at boundaries?
options: Edge inputs are exercised less often in practice

distractor.1: Frequency of use does not cause the faults — off-by-one logic does.
distractor.2: Middles pass even with off-by-one faults; only edge values expose them.
distractor.3: Tests should cover the middle too, but edges catch more.

explanation: Classic slips are > versus >=, a forgotten -1/+1, or a counter started at 1 instead of 0; only edge values expose them.

prompt: Java assertions work out of the box with java TestSuite.
confirm: You must run java -ea or assertions are silently skipped.
explanation: Assertions are disabled by default in Java. Without -ea every test passes even when the code is wrong, which is the classic trap.

prompt: Match each check to its correct assertion form.
explanation: Reals need tolerance, Java strings need .equals, and Python Booleans read most clearly asserted directly.
